To scorn someone or something means to treat them as completely unworthy of your respect, time, or serious attention — because you believe they are beneath you, worthless, or deeply inferior. It is not simply disliking something. Scorn goes further: it combines contempt (a feeling that something is low and worthless) with a sense of superiority (a feeling that you are far above it). When you scorn something, you are not just pushing it away — you are looking down on it.

Think of scorn as sitting at the coldest, most dismissive end of the scale of negative feelings. When you dislike something, you simply do not enjoy it. When you despise something, you feel a strong internal revulsion. But when you scorn it, you feel all of that plus a quiet, powerful sense that it is so beneath you, it barely deserves your notice. There is a certain haughtiness — a feeling of "I am far too good for this" — embedded in the word.

This is why scorn does not always look like anger. In fact, the most cutting expressions of scorn are often calm and cold. A person can scorn someone with a single raised eyebrow, a quiet dismissal, or simply by walking away without a word. That coldness is part of what makes scorn so powerful — and so cutting to the person on the receiving end.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

Scorning a person means regarding them with contempt — treating them as someone inferior, undeserving, or beneath your dignity. For example: "She scorned him for his cowardice." This means she looked down on him with contempt because of how he behaved. She did not just dislike him — she saw him as something low.

Scorning an idea, offer, or suggestion means rejecting it with contempt — as if it is not even worth your consideration. For example: "He scorned the very idea of asking for help." This means he dismissed the idea completely, as if it were beneath him even to entertain it. The rejection here is not polite or neutral; it is wrapped in disdain.
What Scorning Looks Like in Real Life

Scorn can be expressed in many ways — through sharp, dismissive words; through a cold, superior tone of voice; through body language like a curled lip or a contemptuous glance; or even through silence, choosing not to respond because the person or idea is not considered worth engaging with.

Importantly, scorning is not always loud or aggressive. Some of the most devastating expressions of scorn are quiet — a calm, cutting dismissal that communicates "you are not even worth my anger." This quiet version can feel even more humiliating to the person being scorned, because the scorner does not see them as a serious enough threat or presence to warrant a strong reaction.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Hate is a strong negative emotion, but hate does not require a sense of superiority. You can hate someone who is powerful, threatening, or equal to you. Scorn, by contrast, always looks downward — the one scorning considers themselves above the one being scorned.

Mock refers to making fun of someone, but mocking is an action — a specific behavior. Scorn is more of the attitude or feeling that can lead to mocking, but scorn itself is broader and colder than just making fun.

Despise is perhaps the closest word to scorn. The key difference is that despise leans more toward the internal feeling, while scorn is more about both feeling and openly showing or expressing that feeling. You can despise someone quietly in your heart; scorn tends to be more visible, more expressed.

Reject simply means to say no to something, without any particular emotion attached. You can reject an offer politely and respectfully. But when you scorn an offer, you reject it with contempt — as if it were an insult that you were even presented with it.

Disdain is the word most closely synonymous with scorn. They are very similar. If there is a subtle shade of difference, it is that disdain can sometimes feel more reserved and internal, while scorn tends to be more open and actively expressed.
An Important Nuance: Scorn Can Be Justified or Unjust

Scorn is not inherently a negative act — it depends entirely on whether it is deserved. A person can rightly scorn dishonesty, cruelty, or cowardice — looking down on those things with contempt is a morally understandable response. In literature and everyday speech, scorn is sometimes portrayed as noble or dignified when directed at something that truly deserves contempt.

On the other hand, a person can scorn others unfairly — looking down on someone because of their poverty, their background, or their social status. In that case, scorn becomes cruelty. The word itself carries no judgment about whether the scorn is right or wrong — it simply describes the act of looking down on someone or something with contempt.

You will often encounter the phrase "not to be scorned" (or "nothing to be scorned at"), which means something is actually quite good or valuable and should not be dismissed. For example: "A salary of $70,000 is not to be scorned." This means: do not look down on it — it is genuinely worth respecting. This phrase is a reminder that scorn, when misapplied, causes you to unfairly undervalue something real and good.

To scorn something or someone is to reject or regard them with open contempt — treating them as so inferior, worthless, or beneath you that they are not worthy of your serious respect or attention, and making that feeling known.
